en: Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhànrán of Bīlíng during the Táng Dynasty.
Regarding the initial explanation within the section on "perceiving objects," there is first a general explanation, followed by a detailed explanation through the opening of chapters.
First, concerning the word "various" (zhū): my own commentary states that "not one" refers to a multitude. Although that which arises is many, it is not...
One hundred and forty [points] emerge.
To give rise to that which is not in accordance with principle is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, the subsequent section provides a further explanation of the term "view."
Among these one hundred and forty [views],
each gives rise to a specific view that is all logically untenable;
therefore, they are called "false."
Now, regarding those who listen to and study [the teachings] equally:
they debate errors and non-vision,
yet those who listen and study claim for themselves that they have a reliable basis.

To take this meaning as being like life is to disparage those who practice contemplation by calling them "unrealized"; to take this meaning as being like death is [to disparage those who have realized it].
Zhuangzi said: "Where there is discourse, there is life;
where there is no discourse, there is death."
Now, those who practice meditation at a lower level and cultivate contemplation look inward to contemplate principles;
they claim their own feelings have attained penetration and consider this a sublime awakening,
while they denigrate those who study through learning as being like "those who wait by a stump."
What he calls "sentiment" refers to the nature of sentiment, not to deluded sentiment.
Regarding what he calls "clinging to the stump," it is like the story of a farmer in the state of Song.
In a field there was a rabbit that struck a stump and died;
thereafter, he abandoned his plowing and constantly guarded this stump,
hoping that another rabbit might appear.
A bystander advised them, yet they were even more unwilling to desist.
Thus, it is commonly transmitted in worldly tradition that those who persist in their delusion are called "those who guard the stump.
These two individuals originally possessed the two types of spiritual faculties: faith and dharma.
Because they do not understand the underlying intent and thus mutually refute one another,
and because their views are not yet fully established,
it is impossible to determine who is the refuter and who is the refuted.
It is not that each [position] has its own specific obstruction because of the view of arising;
rather, we now evaluate them and declare both to be erroneous.
If one views it as departing...
This provides a brief indication of the arising of views.
Both the questions and the answers are inexhaustible;
the first [section] concerns the inexhaustibility of the questions.
If one explains the following as answering an infinite regress,
it is called "shooting crookedly," which serves as a metaphor for posing questions ad infinitum.
As the Book says:
It was like Hou Yi’s skill in archery;
it was like the nine years of the great flood under Yao,
when seven suns appeared simultaneously.
"Yi shot down six of them.
This, too, is an exaggerated claim by calligraphers.
It further states:
For example, Yang Youji was a master archer;
from a distance of a hundred paces, he could shoot through the leaves of a tree and hit the mark one hundred times in succession.
While out hunting with King Xiang of Chu, he saw a troop of monkeys circling a tree.
The king commanded his attendants to shoot at them,
but the troop of monkeys leaped and bounded even more violently.
The king then commanded Yi Ji to shoot at them.
The monkey then embraced the tree and wailed long and loud.
Seeing this is the vision produced by meditative cultivation (dhyāna);
hearing the name is the vision produced by learning (śruta).
Because he possesses these two qualities,
he differs from those aforementioned groups who merely study, practice meditation, or lack insight;
therefore, his questioning of others is like an archer shooting at a circling bird.
Following the flow of the phrasing, I have cited only one aspect for now.
In full, it should be said: it is like shooting with a curve, encircling birds and beasts so that no flying creature or running beast fails to lose its way.
By means of this, those who have developed insight and are well-versed in names can shatter those who are habituated to meditation and devoid of views,
just as one causes a bird in flight to lose its way.
It can refute those who hold views regarding learning,
just as it causes a runner to lose their way;
this applies to all one hundred and forty-one [points] in the same manner.
Regarding "chuō" (綽),
Guo Pu states that it means "broad and generous."
A poem says: "Vast and ample," like shooting at the great void;
this metaphor illustrates that the response is inexhaustible.
This is precisely to distinguish those who lack insight from those who practice meditation and study;
for both of these attain their realization through training,
whereas the arising of insight differs in that it is born from meditative concentration.
This section below clarifies that the causes are different.
To illustrate, an example is provided:
"The practice of faith is like [the understanding] derived from hearing."
The practice of the Dharma is like meditative concentration based on causes;
it should be understood through hearing and reflection.
As for those who are eloquent and skilled in debate and inquiry:
Those who have attained insight are well able to engage in question and answer, resembling those with the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
There are those who possess such marvelous penetration that their refutations and reconciliations are like the mastery of sublime principles.
These two belong to [the category of] views and are not related to realization through deliberation.
Regarding the passage below beginning with "Those who practice meditation in the South are few," etc.,
this is the formal refutation.
The former passage refers to the territory of Qi, where the regions were separated;
here, it distinguishes the presence or absence of those who perceive [the truth] based on their location.
As for what is called the "True Way":
Those who produce insight through meditation are confused;
those who speak of *dhāraṇī* and produce insight through hearing are confused.
As for the phrase "dark regarding the knowledge of persons," etc.:
Those ignorant ones are blind regarding the discernment of people;
they judge those who have attained insight and assign them to high positions,
even claiming such a state to be the stage of Buddhahood where there is no further birth.
Alternatively, some may lack faith and judge [the person] to be a ghost or insane;
others judge them to be neither.
Now, the following passage concludes that they are neither insane nor noble (ārya).
From "following the husband" down to "possessed by ghosts," it is explained that these are neither madness nor sainthood;
because their seeing belongs to the nature of wisdom, it is called "seeing-wisdom.
In the general discussion below, within the section clarifying the intent of the coming of the vision of objects, [this point is established].
Regarding the statement that "the two meanings are numerous":
this refers to the cases where insight has already arisen within dhyāna, and where both dhyāna and insight arise together;
these two instances are numerous.
If one first gives rise to insight (*vipaśyanā*) and only afterwards gives rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this case is rare;
it is not that it does not exist at all, which is why it is said to be "rare."
Now, the intent of this passage does not concern chronological sequence;
rather, it examines these views collectively while also distinguishing their differences.
Therefore, it speaks of "more or less."
For example, the various dhyānas are explained below as being different in their preceding and succeeding stages of realization.
As for the statement that "the various dhyānas universally give rise to [insight]," this refers collectively to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.
Regarding those who attain [the path] in the sixth and ninth stages,
it is as in the two previous meanings;
even in the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya), there is the sense of generating the outflow-free (anāsrava) state.
However, it does not equal the abundance produced by relying on dhyāna;
therefore, it is said to be "few.
Thus, one uses this example to discern that dhyāna has already been developed.

The six stages consist of the four dhyānas, the intermediate state, and the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). The nine stages consist of these [six] plus the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
To add three further emptinesses above the preceding six is a judgment based on the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-śāstra* (Cheng lun);
it is not the intended meaning of the present text.
If one follows the Abhidharma, one takes the "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) stage while excluding the dhyāna of the desire realm; thus,
it should be said that six stages and nine stages universally give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava),
yet the "not-yet-reached" gives rise to it only slightly.
In other stages, however, they are more numerous.
Nevertheless, this cited example is somewhat inconsistent.
If one were to say that both the dhyāna and the untainted [path] arise together...
Furthermore, there are many instances where one first attains dhyāna and subsequently gives rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava) state;
however, the case where one attains the outflow-free state first and subsequently gives rise to dhyāna is rare.
Thus, it somewhat resembles the state of *sāmayikī-kṣānti*.
Although this resemblance to *sāmayikī-kṣānti* is merely a provisional description,
meditation (*dhyāna*) and the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*), despite having a sequence of priority and posteriority, are nonetheless similar.
Furthermore, it is not entirely identical to the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*); there are differences in their degree and sequence.
This will be clarified below regarding the reduction and increase [of these qualities].
Regarding the phrase "being able to rectify oneself," this means that by consulting the sūtras and śāstras and encountering virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra),
one is able to personally rectify and restrain the errors of one's own views.
One merely eliminates the grasping at inherent nature, not the essence of the view itself.
Since views arise from dhyāna, those who attain dhyāna are few;
yet even those who attain dhyāna and give rise to views are able to exercise self-restraint.
Therefore, it is said that [the Dharma] is difficult to encounter.
To nourish right view and refine the mind is precisely this meaning.
Regarding "the true Dharma" and so forth:
The *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* is cited as scriptural authority to prove the person who is difficult to encounter;

the sūtras and śāstras sought through the realization of the true Dharma are cited as scriptural authority for the teaching; and the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is cited as scriptural authority for the realization.
It is already difficult enough to find a person who has realized the truth and can preach the true Dharma;
how much more so for an audience of those attached to views to receive the true Dharma from such a teacher.
To enter the correct path from the erroneous and to refine the mind by transforming its attachments is called "difficult to attain.
Regarding "dense forest" (*gahana*) and so forth, it means to drag and pull [the mind].
It may also mean "to drag.
The *Zilin* states:
"To pull while lying down."
Birth and death are like a dense forest;
false views are like crooked wood.
This is because one has neither encountered a teacher nor disciplined oneself.
If the mind that perceives does not cease, it is difficult to transcend birth and death,
just like a warped piece of wood.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 38, states:
If the mind is crooked and deviant, it is difficult to attain liberation.
It is like dragging a log through a dense forest; that which is curved is difficult to extract.
Next, in the section explaining the opening chapter:
Regarding the tenets of the three [categories of] persons:
the speculative views of all outsiders do not exceed those of the two gods and the three sages.
As for the "two gods":
This refers to the deity Maheśvara and the deity Viṣṇu— also called Vainateya or Vairāja.
This is translated as "Pervasive Victory," "Pervasive Distress," or "Pervasive Purity."
The Āgamas state:
"This is a deity of the form realm.
The Abhidharmakośa states:
The third dhyāna is the Peak Heaven (Bhavāgra). Jingying says:
"It abides at the extreme limit of the desire realm."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The god Śuddhāvāsakāyika has four arms; he holds a conch and a wheel and rides upon a garuḍa.
He possesses great supernatural power, yet is prone to anger and violence."
At that time, people, fearing his majesty, proceeded to honor him with even greater reverence.
Regarding the account of the one man at the beginning of the kalpa who held back the waters of the ocean with his thousand heads and two thousand hands,
it is recorded in the commentary on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The Commentary states:
"Of the twenty-four hands and one thousand heads, one is missing; he is born by transformation upon the water.
In the center [of the water] is a thousand-petaled lotus flower."
Within the flower there was light, like ten thousand suns shining together.
Because of this flower, the Brahmā King descended to be born.
Having been born, he thought to himself:
"Why is it empty and devoid of sentient beings?
While he was thinking this, eight devaputras who were destined to be born in this world from other realms suddenly appeared through miraculous birth.
The eight heavenly kings are the parents of all sentient beings.
Brahmā is the parent of the eight heavenly kings. Viṣṇu is the parent of Brahmā.
Tracing back to the ultimate source, he is revered by the world;
therefore, he is called "World-Honored One" (Lokanātha).
As the *Piyū jīng* (*Avadāna-sūtra*) says:
Various outsiders maintain that the Brahmā King gave birth to the four castes:
from his mouth were born the Brāhmaṇas; from his arms, the Kṣatriyas;
from his flanks, the Vaiśyas; and from his feet, the Śūdras.
The Madhyama Āgama states:
"Kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and artisans are called the four castes."
The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:
"Kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, and śūdras—
though their occupations differ slightly, they are all collectively termed 'commoners' (*pṛthagjana*)."
Maheśvara is here translated as Mahādeva;
he is the deity at the summit of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu),
possessing three eyes and eight arms, riding a white ox and holding a white fly-whisk.
Possessing great majestic power capable of overturning the world,
he takes the World-Honored One as the fundamental basis for his transformations.
As the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
In the realm of Maheśvara there dwells a bodhisattva named Maheśvara;
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that he is a bodhisattva of the tenth stage.
Up to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, these are Bodhisattvas of the first stage.
One should know that the traces of all these devas are for the sake of ordinary beings; fundamentally, they are great manifestations of expedient power.
As for what are called the "three seers":
The first is Kapila, which translates as "Yellow-Headed," because his head was like the color of gold.
It is also said:
His head and face were both golden in color;
he was named for this reason.
Fearing that his body would die, he went to the god Īśvara to inquire about it.
The gods commanded him to go to Mount Piṇḍa to fetch āmalaka fruits, saying that by eating them his life could be prolonged.
Having eaten them, he was transformed within the forest into a stone as large as a bed.
Those who could not reach it wrote verses upon the stone to inquire [of him].
Later, he was refuted by the Bodhisattva Dignāga.
His books, verses, and the splitting of rocks,
as well as his attainment of the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), enabled him to know eighty thousand *kalpas* both before and after his own time.
He surveyed the world to see who was fit to be delivered.
He saw a brahmin named Śūlika wandering among the people and asked him:
"Are you playing? He replied, "Yes."
After another two thousand years had passed,
he asked:
"Are you able to cultivate the Path?"
Answer: Yes,
for it explains the three types of suffering.
First is internal suffering, such as hunger and thirst;
second is external suffering, such as tigers and wolves;
third is celestial suffering, such as wind and rain.
The discourse consists of one hundred thousand verses and is called the *Sāṃkhya-śāstra*.
This term means "calculation" (*saṃkhyā*).
It elucidates that the effect exists within the cause by means of the twenty-five principles (*tattva*).
The principle of "calculating the one" as the fundamental tenet is expressed through the twenty-five truths (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*). First,
from the primordial darkness (*avyakta*), intellect (*buddhi*) is produced.
Beyond eighty thousand kalpas in the past, it was dark and unknowable;
one merely perceives the initial arising of the first intermediate state (*antarābhava*),
constantly recollecting and contemplating it through the power of past lives (*pūrvajātismara*).
It is called the "Primal Darkness" (mūla-tattva),
also known as the "World-Nature" (jagat-prakṛti).
This means that the sentient beings of the world exist by virtue of this primal darkness.
This is the very nature of the world;
it is also called spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Because it has no origin, awakening arises from it.
It is also called "Great," which refers to the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Next, regarding the phrase "the 'I'-mind arises from awareness":
this is the "I" of self-conceit (*māna*), not the "I" of a permanent self (*ātman*).
That is the third truth: from my mind arise form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch;
from these five objects arise the five great elements, namely the four great elements and space.
The subtle and coarse atoms combine to form the great elements;
therefore, it is said that "the great arise from the atoms.
However, there are differences regarding the quantity of these great elements that arise.
From sound arises the great element of space;
from sound and touch arise the great element of wind;
from form, sound, and touch arises the great element of fire.
From color, sound, touch, and taste, the water element arises;
from the five sense objects, the earth element arises.
Because the earth element relies upon many sense objects, its power is the weakest.
Even down to the element of space (*ākāśa-mahābhūta*), because it relies on the least amount of matter (*rūpa*), its power is the strongest.
Therefore, when the four wheels form the world, the wheel of space is at the very bottom;
next is wind, then fire, then water, and finally earth.
From the five great elements arise the eleven faculties;
because the faculties such as the eye are capable of cognition,
they are called "faculties" (indriya) and are termed the "five cognitive faculties" (pañca-vijñānendriya).
Because the hands, feet, mouth, anus, and genitals have functional utility, they are called the five organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The mind is the organ of equanimity (*samānendriya*).
Taken together, there are eleven faculties.
Because the mind can take all things as its object, it is called the faculty of equanimity (*samatā-indriya*).
If the five faculties of cognition each employ one of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), [they are established].
That is to say, the sensory object of form constitutes the fire element;
the fire element constitutes the eye faculty;
and the eye faculty, in turn, perceives form.
The empty particles form the ear-faculty;
the ear-faculty, in turn, hears sounds.
Earth forms the nose.
The tongue is formed from water;
the body is formed from wind—
it is also like this.
These twenty-four truths are what belongs to the self (*ātman*);
all are designated as the "truth of the master" (*prabhu-tattva*) based on the spiritual self.
When the subject and object are discussed together, there are twenty-five.
Second, the followers of the Sāṃkhya school calculate that [the elements] are all-pervasive in their creation;
however, they maintain that the eye faculty contains a predominance of fire, and so on, up to the body faculty containing a predominance of wind,
as explained in detail in the *Saptati-śāstra* (The Seventy Verses).
Furthermore, among the non-Buddhists, there was a leader of a group who went to the kingdom of Suvarṇabhūmi;
he placed a brazier upon his head and covered his belly with iron leaves,
then beat the drum of debate to summon the monks for a discussion.
There was a monk from East India who engaged in debate with him.
That [opponent] established that the world is eternal.
The monk challenged him, saying:
Now there must necessarily be destruction, for at the time when the world is destroyed, the world necessarily perishes;
therefore, it is known through inference that there is destruction now. He says:
It will certainly not perish, like the mountain of gold and other such [treasures].
At that time, that king sided with those non-Buddhists,
and consequently caused this monk to suffer humiliation by being made to ride a donkey.
The King, out of respect for the non-Buddhist teacher, bestowed seventy *kārṣāpaṇa* of gold upon him;
consequently, he composed a treatise titled the *Saptati-śāstra*, or "Seventy [Verses on] Gold.
Later, Vasubandhu composed the *Saptati-bhāṣya* to extensively refute that school's tenets and to defend the doctrines of the former Buddhist monks.
The King, honoring the former monk, again commanded the people of the kingdom to widely propagate the treatises composed by Vasubandhu;
he caused the corpses of the non-Buddhists and those who had debated the meaning [of the scriptures] to be unearthed,
and their bones were whipped with whips.
That school further maintains that Maheśvara possesses three bodies,
as cited in full in the third fascicle.
Ulūka-sāṃkhya is translated here as Xiuliu-xian (休留仙).
This person would hide in mountain valleys during the day to compose sutras and books,
and travel about at night to preach the Dharma and transform sentient beings;
because he was like that bird, he received this name.
It is also called "Eye-foot" (Akṣapāda), for he possessed three eyes on his feet.
He engaged in debate with the god Maheśvara;
because that god has three eyes on his face, [Akṣapāda] was given that name by comparison to his feet.
That person appeared eight hundred years before the Buddha and also attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
He composed a treatise consisting of one hundred thousand verses, titled *Vaiśeṣika*.
This is called *Amṛta* (Unconquerable).
It takes the six truths as its primary tenet.
The first is *dravyasatya*, which is translated here as the "truth of the primary substance" (*zhuti*).
That is to say, the five great elements, time, space, the deity, and the mind—
these nine are that upon which all things depend;
therefore, they are called the lords.
The second is *guṇa*, here translated as "attributes" (*yidi*).

This refers to the five sense objects, such as form, along with their qualities of identity and difference, separation and conjunction, quantity and number, beauty and ugliness, folly and wisdom, love and hatred, suffering and pleasure, diligence and indolence.
These twenty-one [categories] rely upon the aforementioned nine dharmas;
therefore, they are called "relying on the truths" (*satya*).
Third is the truth of ritual action (*karmasatya*), which is here translated as the "truth of performance."
This refers to such actions as looking up and down, bending and stretching, entering and exiting, going and coming;
therefore, they are called "formative activities" (*saṃskāra*). Fourth is *sammuti-sacca*, which is translated here as the "truth of conventional designations."
This means that all phenomena are collectively subsumed into one great existence;
therefore, it is called the "Truth of the Totality" (saṃgraha-satya).
Fifth is the *vishiṣa-satya*, which is translated as the "Truth of Particular Characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-satya*).
This means that the myriad phenomena are each distinct;
therefore, they are called "distinct characteristics" (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa). Sixth is *māparyāta*.
That is to say, they hold that atoms forming a jar do not obstruct one another;
and regarding the qualities (*guṇa*), they consider it a virtuous practice to bathe three times a day and repeatedly make offerings to fire.
Furthermore, they calculate that the waters of the Ganges can extinguish karmic obstacles;
thus, one must wash three times.
They also claim that fire is the mouth of the gods.
Because the gods consume these foods, they are called "mouths of heaven.
At two times [of the day], one burns incense, ghee, and other offerings,
causing their fragrance to ascend to heaven as an act of worship, in the hope of seeking blessings and extinguishing transgressions.
Third is Leisha-po (Laiṣava), which is translated as "asceticism.
They do not know the timing of liberation,
and they take calculation as their holy dharma.
The scripture he composed also consists of one hundred thousand verses and is titled the *Nirgrantha*.
This person has severed the fetters and takes the six obstructions and four turbidities as his doctrine.
He calculates that within the cause there is both fruit and no fruit.
The thesis is that [the self] is both identical and different.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, four positions are fully set forth;
three are as previously mentioned, with the addition of the son of Mṛṣāvādin (Ajita Keśakambalin).
I do not yet know the timing of his appearance in the world, nor the number of sūtras he composed.
Calculating from the perspective of the causal stage, he held the thesis that there is neither fruit within the cause nor is there no fruit;
it is neither identical with nor different from it.
Regarding the six obstructions mentioned by the Nirgranthas,
the *Upāyahṛdaya-śāstra* states:
first, the obstruction of non-vision.
Second, the obstacle of delusion;
third, the obstacle of suffering;
fourth, the obstacle of the exhaustion of life.
Fifth, the obstacle of the five natures;
sixth, the obstacle of names and words.
Regarding the "four turbidities":
That is to say: hatred, pride, greed, and deceit.
Furthermore, the *Upāyahr̥daya-śāstra* states that the tenets of the Ulūka and Kapila schools differ from this.
That treatise further contains the Naya-mati system of ten truths. Furthermore,
regarding the two types of wisdom— those derived from hearing and reflection— there are eight [truths] pertaining to the wisdom derived from hearing.
First, astronomy;
second, mathematics;
third, medicine.
The four incantations and the four Vedas constitute eight;
thus, there are eight types of wisdom consisting of reflection.
First, the Heaven of Long Life;
second, the Heaven of the Constellations;
third, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Up to the Heaven of Control over Others' Emanations— these are the eight.
Ascetic practice is itself the practice of the long-lived devas.
There are six practices in total, such as scorching the body with the five fires:
first, self-starvation;
second, throwing oneself into deep pools.
Third, entering fire;
fourth, throwing oneself down;
fifth, remaining silent.
Sixth, the observance of the precepts for chickens, dogs, and so forth.
Some say that this is intended to signify a superior asceticism compared to that of the śramaṇas.
To say that a śramaṇa baring his shoulder is the same as being naked,
or that a śramaṇa shaving his head is the same as plucking out his hair,
is a profound lack of discernment.
They take asceticism as their primary principle and practice all forms of suffering;
they do not consider themselves superior to those śramaṇas and others. Now, it is said that they are superior in terms of their own specific characteristics.
Because the suffering seen by those teachers was not yet acute,
they plucked out their hair and so forth;
because they did not yet throw themselves from cliffs, I threw myself from a cliff.
I entered the fire because I saw those three washings;
I threw myself down because I saw those five ripenings.
This is according to the *Yuanyou jing* (Sūtra on the Original Causes) of the non-Buddhists.
There was a bhikṣu who encountered bandits and had his robes stolen.
A brāhmaṇa saw this and imitated it all,
even going so far as to strip naked and throw himself down.
As will be explained later,
for these reasons, they establish the tenets of the non-Buddhist schools (tīrthika).
Furthermore, they reckon such things as the horse sacrifice to be a source of constant merit and so forth.
Thus, the Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra states:
"He slaughtered four thousand horses, removed their five internal organs,
and offered them as an inner gift of the seven treasures to the brāhmaṇas."
It is the same with the inner treasure of killing. Furthermore,
if one were to shoot arrows in the four directions and, upon reaching the furthest limits where horses can run, spread treasures there to give as alms to brahmins—
were one to kill all the sentient beings within that much land [the merit would be greater].
If one burns everything,
or pays homage to all trees,
or pays homage to all mountain deities.
Thus, there are twenty-six such heterodox views in total.
Furthermore, there are outsiders who reckon five things as eternal:
first, that the principle of emptiness is eternal because it is not non-existent; [and so forth].
Second, it is eternal because it is neither produced nor destroyed across the two times.
Third, it is eternal because it exists in all directions throughout the ten quarters.
Fourth, it is eternal because atoms are extremely subtle and thus cannot be further divided.
Fifth, nirvāṇa is eternal because it is unchanging.
Question:
